quiz.question: Why is property a data descriptor, and why does that matter?
options: This pattern uses Base.value.setter(fset) which returns a new property using Base.value.fget and the new fset.
Each call to .setter(), .getter(), or .deleter() creates a brand-new property object.
A __slots__ entry without assignment always has a setter (the slot descriptor handles it); there is no built-in way to make a slot read-only without a property.
A descriptor is any object that defines __get__, __set__, or __delete__.
quiz.explanation: A descriptor is any object that defines __get__, __set__, or __delete__. A data descriptor defines both __get__ and __set__. Python's attribute lookup gives data descriptors priority over the instance __dict__.

quiz.question: What happens when you access a property on the class rather than an instance?
options: cached_property is a non-data descriptor — it only defines __get__, not __set__.
This pattern uses Base.value.setter(fset) which returns a new property using Base.value.fget and the new fset.
Yes. A property on a metaclass controls attribute access on the class object itself (since a class is an instance of its metaclass).
When obj is None (i.e., accessed via the class), property.__get__ returns the property object itself.
quiz.explanation: When obj is None (i.e., accessed via the class), property.__get__ returns the property object itself. This is how @classmethod and @staticmethod also behave — the descriptor's __get__ receives None for obj and returns itself (or a bound method for classmethod). This is useful for introspection — you can access fget, fset, fdel, and __doc__ via the class.

quiz.question: How does @prop.setter create a new property rather than mutating the existing one?

Yes. A property on a metaclass controls attribute access on the class object itself (since a class is an instance of its metaclass).

quiz.explanation: Each call to .setter(), .getter(), or .deleter() creates a brand-new property object. This is intentional — in Python's data model, class attributes should be treated as immutable after class creation. The pattern works because: Each decorator call returns a new property, and the x name in the class namespace is rebound.

quiz.question: How does cached_property differ from property at the descriptor protocol level?
options: Each call to .setter(), .getter(), or .deleter() creates a brand-new property object.
Yes. A property on a metaclass controls attribute access on the class object itself (since a class is an instance of its metaclass).
This pattern uses Base.value.setter(fset) which returns a new property using Base.value.fget and the new fset.
cached_property is a non-data descriptor — it only defines __get__, not __set__.
quiz.explanation: cached_property is a non-data descriptor — it only defines __get__, not __set__. This is deliberate: after the first call, it stores the result in obj.__dict__[attr]. On subsequent accesses, Python's attribute lookup finds the value in obj.__dict__ before consulting the class for a non-data descriptor, so cached_property.__get__ is never called again — the cache hit is essentially free.

quiz.explanation: Yes. A property on a metaclass controls attribute access on the class object itself (since a class is an instance of its metaclass). This is an advanced pattern used in ORMs and frameworks to allow class-level descriptor access (e.g., MyModel.field_name returns a query expression, not the field value).
